The Committee’s decision to lower the target range to 1-1/2 to 1-3/4 percent and to maintain ample reserves via Treasury bill purchases and repo operations is a textbook dovish response to a mixed outlook: labor markets remain strong, but business fixed investment and exports are weak and inflation is below target. The literature supports this tilt. Investment is sensitive to the user cost of capital and to financing conditions; easing short-term rates should support capex and inventory investment, particularly where internal funds matter (evidence on inventory investment sensitivity to financing constraints in Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994). With market-based inflation compensation low and survey expectations little changed, New Keynesian models in which expected inflation is a key driver of current inflation (e.g., Galí and Gertler; Woodford; Christiano, Eichenbaum, and Evans) justify accommodation to help re-anchor outcomes near the symmetric 2 percent objective. Moreover, empirical work showing that monetary policy affects real activity through interest-rate channels (e.g., Sims/Zha VAR evidence; Romer and Romer narrative approach) is consistent with the FOMC’s emphasis on ensuring smooth money market functioning to safeguard transmission. Two dissents and acknowledged uncertainties temper the tone, but the balance of risks and the literature’s guidance on weak investment and subdued inflation make the overall message moderately positive and cautiously accommodative.
